title: Industry Structure, Competitive Moat & External Learning Hub
web_title: 4. Industry Structure, Competitive Moat & External Learning Hub
book_title: Chapter 4: The Battlefield — Rivals, Switching Costs & Moat Reality
question: Does PCBL own a durable competitive advantage in carbon black and in its new chemistries, or does it sell a commodity into an industry that has built more capacity than it can fill?

epigraph.quote: “While the industry continues to be in overcapacity, we believe that structurally, we will be able to take some price increases with value-added products.”
epigraph.author: Nilesh Koul, Managing Director, PCBL Chemical, Q4 FY26 earnings call, 30 April 2026

web_blocks.html: A moat is the reason a business keeps earning more than its cost of capital after rivals have noticed the profits. PCBL has to be tested in three separate arenas. The first is rubber-grade carbon black, where it is India's largest producer. The second is phosphonate and specialty chemicals through Aquapharm. The third is battery materials, where it has a pilot plant and no named customer. This chapter maps who competes in each arena and what sets the margin per tonne. It then weighs the evidence for and against a moat and ends with an independent verdict on how wide the moat is. Chapter 3 covered how PCBL sells and Chapter 5 tests whether management's promises held, so here the question is purely competitive.

web_blocks.takeaway: India is adding capacity at 7.9% a year against demand growth of 3.7%, which is more than double the pace. Unless demand surprises or plants close, the industry gets emptier before it gets fuller.

web_blocks.html: The published Indian utilisation row needs care because it does not survive arithmetic. Production over capacity is 1.47 / 2.10 = 70% for FY2025, and domestic demand over capacity is 1.17 / 2.10 = 56%, while the report prints 57%. For FY2030F the same report prints 70%, yet the arithmetic gives 57% on production (1.75 / 3.07) and 46% on demand (1.40 / 3.07) [3]. The two printed labels look transposed. We therefore treat FY2025 utilisation as a range. The range runs from 56% (domestic demand against capacity) to 70% (production including exports against capacity), with the published 57% at the low end. We read the forecast as a fall, because capacity grows at 7.9% while production grows at 3.5%. On either reading PCBL fills its plants better than the industry. It sold 596,262 t against 790 KTPA of year-end nameplate in FY2025, or 75.5% (my calc) [9][3]. Management accepts the structural point: “the industry continues to be in overcapacity” [36].

Himadri earned ₹1,006 Cr of EBITDA from a carbon black base 3.6x smaller than PCBL's 900 KTPA and kept ROCE at 32% against PCBL's 8%. Orion and Cabot show the same split globally, where rubber grades are shrinking and specialty carries the profit.

web_blocks.html: Two lessons follow. First, scale alone has not delivered superior returns in this industry. PCBL's capacity rose 46% between FY2021 and FY2026 (603 kt to 880 kt, my calc) while its ROCE fell from 17% to 8% [4]. Second, the profit is migrating to grades that need qualification. That is why the rest of this chapter looks hard at the specialty share. It was 11.3% of PCBL's carbon black volume in FY2026 (69,635 t of 618,956 t) [14].

web_blocks.title: How the margin per tonne is set

web_blocks.html: Carbon black is made by partly burning a heavy oil residue (carbon black feedstock, CBFS) in a furnace. The fine black powder goes into tyres and the hot tail gas runs a co-generation plant. About 75% of PCBL's CBFS comes from the US Gulf Coast, and about 40% of its sales are exported [36]. The margin is therefore the spread between selling price and feedstock. Five things adjust that spread: the contract formula, spot exposure, inventory timing, product mix and power. Orion describes the same architecture, with indexed contracts covering about 65% of its volume [60].

web_blocks.takeaway: Only two of the six levers (product mix and co-generation) are structural. The other four move with crude, freight and Russian or Chinese supply. So a high quarterly EBITDA per tonne is weak evidence of a moat until it survives a crude reversal. Chapter 5 tracks the history.

web_blocks.html: The Q2 FY27 power line shows how the credit works. At the prior-year tariff of ₹3.76, the 108 MU sold would have earned ₹40.6 Cr. At ₹5.34 they earned ₹57.7 Cr, a ₹17 Cr uplift in one quarter that has nothing to do with carbon black pricing (my calc) [18]. It is a genuine advantage of the furnace process. Even so, 70.6% of standalone power sales go to related parties [3], so it should be read as a stable earnings floor rather than as proof of pricing power.

web_blocks.title: Customers, pricing power and switching costs

web_blocks.html: The Integrated Report discloses that carbon black customers who each exceed 10% of revenue contributed ₹1,958.55 Cr in FY2026 and ₹2,429.40 Cr in FY2025 [3]. That is 30.1% of carbon black revenue and 23.9% of group revenue in FY2026, against 35.7% and 28.9% in FY2025 (my calc). Three customers above 10% of ₹8,189 Cr would need at least ₹2,457 Cr, so the arithmetic means no more than two such customers exist. Names are not disclosed. Tyre makers are therefore few, large and able to dual-source. They say their own price increases are “not fully passing through” to the market (MD, 2 Nov 2026) [40]. ICRA expects domestic tyre demand to rise 5–7% in FY2027 with operating margins contracting on crude [45]. This is a customer base that will resist further price increases.

Switching costs are real but modest. A new grade or plant has to be approved by each tyre maker, so the Chennai greenfield ran at about 50% in its first full quarter. It reached 60% by Q4 FY24 [26][28]. Approval slows an entrant. It does not stop a tyre maker from buying a qualified grade from a second supplier at a lower price. The sharpest evidence is PCBL's own behaviour. In Q2 FY27 it let carbon black volume fall 17.0% to 134,180 t because spot prices were not worth taking, and the CFO said “we are not chasing volumes. We would rather keep this capacity spare” [40]. The MD described the competition as “some people are chasing volume and I assume some degree of cash” [40]. A producer with a wide moat does not cede 17% of volume to keep price discipline. It holds both.

web_blocks.takeaway: PCBL's carbon black earns its margin with no anti-dumping shield. The 2026 relief from Russian and Chinese imports comes from Russian refinery outages and firmer Chinese coal-tar costs, both of which can reverse. The only live trade remedy belongs to Aquapharm, and it is not yet confirmed in force.

web_blocks.html: Phosphonates are scale inhibitors and chelating agents used in detergents, water treatment and oil fields. On the acquisition call in November 2023 the Managing Director, Kaushik Roy, put the global market at about 250 kt and Aquapharm's capacity at about 130 kt. He ranked it as “one of the top two players”, while the Chairman said Italmatch was “1% or 2% higher than us” [27]. By Q1 FY25 the claim was “approximately 24% of global market share, excluding China” [29]. By the September 2025 Investor Day it was “amongst Top 3” [11]. A third-party estimate puts the market at US$1.03 bn in 2025 growing 4.65% a year [63]. The wording drift matters less than the economics. In the DGTR record, the domestic industry (Aquapharm and Excel Industries) reported financial losses, cash losses and negative return on capital employed on HEDP and ATMP. That covered April 2024–March 2025, when Chinese landed prices were below its cost of sales [57]. The commodity end of phosphonates therefore has no pricing power today. The value sits in blends, green chelates and customer-approved formulations.

Green chelates (GLDA and MGDA, which replace phosphonates in some detergents) show how far the moat is from proven. The Chairman's 2023 aim was to raise them “20x over the next 5 years” from 3,300 t [27]. Capacity is about 4,000 t, or 1.2x, three years in, with expansion deferred until product approvals arrive [36]. Oil and gas is where Aquapharm holds under 1% of the global market and where volume fell 19% in FY2026 [29][36]. Customers named at acquisition (P&G, Unilever, Henkel, Reckitt) approve suppliers slowly and rarely switch once approved [27][83]. That is a genuine barrier, but it has not yet protected EBITDA per kg. FY2026 Aquapharm EBITDA was ₹162 Cr on ₹1,443 Cr revenue, an 11.2% margin against the 20% described at signing (see Chapter 5) [14][27].

PCBL is an entrant at sample stage. No moat exists here yet, only an option. Management's own timeline moved from “ready in the next few months” (29 Apr 2025) to first samples (2 Nov 2026) [32][40].

web_blocks.takeaway: Qualification friction and cost position are real, but they slow rivals. They do not stop pricing pressure in an industry that adds capacity twice as fast as demand. Returns equal to the cost of debt are what a narrow moat looks like once the cycle turns.

web_blocks.html: Our verdict is that PCBL has a narrow moat in Indian rubber-grade carbon black, resting on port-side scale, co-generation and customer approvals. It has no demonstrated moat yet in phosphonates or battery materials. We judge it more likely than not (roughly two in three) that the carbon black franchise earns its cost of capital through a full cycle. That view rests on mid-cycle EBITDA per tonne in the high teens of thousands of rupees. The FY2023–FY2025 history of ₹17,405, ₹20,018 and ₹19,930 supports it [24][6][9]. We judge the chance that it earns above-cost returns by a wide margin as well under one in three unless specialty grows well beyond 11% of volume. That wide-margin case is the one Himadri shows, with its 22% EBITDA margin. Management's thesis is the reverse of Himadri's. Himadri raised margin from 6% to 22% by shifting toward value-added products on a clean balance sheet. PCBL is shifting platforms with about four times EBITDA in net debt.

What would change our mind. We would widen the verdict to moderate on any of three conditions. The first is four consecutive quarters of carbon black EBITDA per tonne at or above ₹17,000 after removing inventory gains and tariff refunds, while volume recovers above 75% of nameplate. The second is that the HEDP and ATMP duty is notified and Aquapharm quarterly EBITDA reaches ₹60 Cr. The third is that a named battery customer completes qualification. We would narrow it to none if FY2027 volume keeps falling at the H1 pace of −8.9% while Indian capacity moves toward 3.07 Mt.

External Learning Hub. Industry primers and data: read the ICRA carbon black sector report for the EU ban on Russian black, India's shift to net exporter and the cost edge over China. Read the ICRA Indian tyre industry report for tyre demand, exports and margin outlook, which drive carbon black volume. The Wikipedia carbon black primer covers grades and uses, and the Birla Carbon site shows the largest Indian competitor's product range. Peers and filings: PCBL's own Integrated Report 2025-26 has the industry data and segment notes used above. The Investor Day deck sets out the FY2030 targets and capacity plan. Orion's 10-K shows indexed contracts and the specialty versus rubber split. Cabot's annual report shows how the global leader's rubber business shrank while specialty grew. Himadri's annual report shows the domestic peer's specialty strategy and returns. Trade policy: the DGTR 2020 carbon black findings list domestic capacity and duty rates, and the European Rubber Journal report records the Finance Ministry's refusal to extend them. The DGTR HEDP and ATMP case page shows how a live Indian anti-dumping case proceeds. Battery realism: the IEEFA study of India's battery incentive scheme shows how little cell capacity has been built. The Group14 BAM-2 page shows what a scaled silicon-carbon anode plant looks like.

The three parallels below are mechanism tests, not comparisons of size. One shows the upside when a carbon-materials peer converts specialty mix into returns. One shows what a levered commodity-chemicals base looks like when margins collapse. One shows how a specialty-chemicals reset follows a cyclical peak.

web_blocks.region_era: India, FY2022–FY2026; coal-tar pitch processor shifting into specialty carbon black and anode materials
web_blocks.mechanism: A commodity carbon-materials processor selling to the same tyre and industrial customers pushed volume into specialty carbon black and value-added carbon materials. It used qualification friction and scale economies, and it funded the expansion from internal earnings rather than debt [62].
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: EBITDA margin rose from 6% (FY2022) through 10%, 15%, 18% to 22% (FY2026). FY2026 EBITDA was ₹1,006 Cr (+19%) and PAT was ₹755 Cr (+36%). ROCE was 32%, ROE 18% and net debt to equity (0.03). Specialty black capacity was 130,000 TPA of 250,000 TPA total [62].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: The same specialty-mix mechanism lifted a peer's margin by 16 points while keeping the balance sheet clean. PCBL's FY2026 EBITDA margin was 13.2% with net debt near 4.2x EBITDA, and much of its non-tyre growth went into lower-value performance grades. The mechanism is therefore available to PCBL but has not yet paid off at group level. Himadri's gains also came off a 6% trough, and it is a peer rather than an independent analogue [14][3].

web_blocks.region_era: UK and US titanium dioxide and performance additives, 2017–2022
web_blocks.mechanism: A commodity-chemicals business carved out with separation debt met an oversupplied, Chinese-supply-driven cycle. Adjusted EBITDA collapsed and restructuring charges and plant closures followed. All debt then moved into current liabilities with a going-concern warning [59].
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: 2022 revenue was $2,173 M and the net loss was $181 M. Adjusted EBITDA was $53 M against $180 M in 2021 (−71%). Total debt was $1,040 M, all classified short-term, up from $946 M. Restructuring, impairment and plant closing costs were $142 M against $68 M. The Pori plant in Finland closed in 2022, and the auditor's report carried a going-concern paragraph [59].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: When EBITDA falls by more than two thirds on a levered base, gearing ratios jump and maturities decide the outcome. PCBL's EBITDA fell 22% in FY2026 (₹1,384 Cr to ₹1,081 Cr) with net debt already near 4x. The direction of the ratio is therefore the same. The asset base, formula-priced customers and ₹448 Cr of promoter warrant money are materially better than Venator's [14][9][28].

web_blocks.region_era: India specialty chemicals, FY2023 peak to FY2024 reset
web_blocks.mechanism: Specialty and fluorochemicals earned record profits in FY2023. Customers then destocked and prices fell while the company kept spending on expansion, so earnings reset sharply despite an unbroken structural-growth narrative [1].
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: FY2024 operating revenue fell 12% to ₹13,139 Cr. EBITDA fell 26% to ₹2,744 Cr (21% margin). PAT fell 38%, from ₹2,162 Cr to ₹1,336 Cr. Chemicals revenue fell 15% to ₹6,297 Cr in a “more protracted inventory destocking cycle”. About ₹1,700 Cr of Chemicals capex was spent during the downturn [1].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: PCBL's FY2024–FY2025 EBITDA per tonne of ₹20,018 and ₹19,930 sat near a cyclical high, and the Aquapharm forecasts were set at that level. FY2026 at ₹14,939 is the reset. SRF kept a 21% EBITDA margin at its trough, while PCBL's was 13.2%. SRF also carried no acquisition debt of comparable size, which makes PCBL's trough harder to absorb [14][6][1].

web_blocks.html: For an owner, the takeaway is that PCBL's carbon black is a good, cost-advantaged business inside a poorly structured industry. Its advantage is narrow enough that returns depend on specialty mix, discipline on spot volume and the balance sheet, not on anti-dumping protection or scale. Chapter 5 now tests whether the key performance indicators and management's record support the specialty-and-solutions story.

book_paragraphs: Let us start with a question I ask about every industrial company: if you gave a smart competitor a billion dollars and five years, could they take the customer? For carbon black the honest answer is that they already have tried. Look at the numbers I laid out in this chapter. India has installed about 2.1 million tonnes of capacity against domestic demand of 1.17 million tonnes. PCBL's own report forecasts capacity of 3.07 million tonnes by 2030, growing at 7.9% a year, while demand grows at 3.7%. So whatever moat PCBL owns, it sits inside an industry in which everybody is building more plant than the market can fill.

Here is a small detective story you should know about, because it will teach you to distrust any single number. The Integrated Report prints India's utilisation as 57% for FY2025 and 70% for FY2030. I divided its own production of 1.47 million tonnes by its own capacity of 2.10 million tonnes and got 70% for FY2025, then did the same for 2030 and got 57%. The two labels are simply swapped. That matters because it changes the headline from a catastrophe today to a slow deterioration tomorrow. PCBL itself ran at about 75% of nameplate in FY2025, so it fills its plants better than the average competitor. But capacity outgrowing production by more than twice the rate means that unless someone closes a plant, the industry gets emptier.

Now walk with me to the factory floor and ask what actually sets the margin. A tyre maker's purchasing manager signs a contract in which the black's price follows a feedstock index, with a lag of a quarter or a month. When crude jumps, as it did when Brent went from about $60 to about $100 between January and March 2026, the producer eats the difference for a few months and then catches up. The Managing Director told investors on 30 April 2026 that the full impact of cost pass-through would show by Q2 FY27, and it did. About a third of volume is sold spot instead, and in Q1 FY27 the Managing Director said, in his own words, “close to a third of our volumes are on the spot market, and our teams monetize this exposure very effectively.” That sentence explains why Q1 FY27 carbon black EBITDA per tonne hit ₹22,900. About ₹70 crore of it was low-cost inventory sold at high prices, which works out to about ₹4,560 per tonne.

So can you call ₹22,900 a moat? I would not, and neither would a careful credit analyst. A moat is the part of the margin that survives when crude falls. Of the six levers I tabulated, only two are structural: product mix and the power from tail gas. Power is a pleasant surprise. At the same tonnage, the tariff rising from ₹3.76 to ₹5.34 per unit gave about ₹17 crore of extra profit in one quarter. But that is a fortunate market price and 70.6% of those power sales go to related parties, so I treat it as a floor rather than a weapon.

Think about the customer's side of the table. The Integrated Report tells us that customers who each exceed 10% of revenue contributed ₹1,958.55 crore in FY2026. I worked out that three such customers would need at least ₹2,457 crore, so there can be no more than two. A handful of tyre giants who can approve a second supplier will always push on price, and in the Q2 FY27 call the Managing Director said tyre makers' own price increases were not fully passing through to their markets. Qualification is a real barrier: PCBL's new Chennai plant took a year to reach 60% utilisation because each tyre company had to approve the grades. But a barrier that slows a newcomer does not stop your customer from buying a qualified grade from someone cheaper.

Which brings me to the most revealing moment in the recent record. In Q2 FY27, PCBL's carbon black volume fell 17.0% to 134,180 tonnes. CFO Raj Gupta explained on 2 November 2026: “We are not chasing volumes. We would rather keep this capacity spare.” Managing Director Nilesh Koul added that “some people are chasing volume and I assume some degree of cash.” I respect the discipline, and the EBITDA per tonne of ₹19,800 in that quarter shows it did not hurt margin. But ask yourself what kind of competitive position lets you give up a sixth of your volume to keep the price. It is the position of a company that has a cost edge worth defending, not one that owns the market.

Let us look more closely at the arena where the profit is moving, which is specialty black. Orion's filing lets us measure it: in 2024 its rubber blacks earned about $282 of EBITDA a tonne and its specialty blacks about $440, which is 1.56 times as much. Cabot's numbers tell the same story from the other side: its rubber business saw sales fall 10.3% and EBIT fall 5.4% in fiscal 2025, which it blamed on weak tyre demand and Asian tyre imports into western regions, while its Performance Chemicals EBIT rose 18% on flat sales. So the global leader is also migrating toward specialty. Where does PCBL stand? Specialty blacks were 11.3% of its volume in FY26. When an analyst asked on 2 November 2026 how much specialty it could sell, Managing Director Nilesh Koul answered, “So on specialty, the capacity that we have is around 75, so we are good to market that. We are tying up more and more resources for raw material, which is feedstock, which is unique for specialty chemicals. So that is the barrier.” Do you see what that sentence reveals? The plant has 132,000 tonnes of nameplate, but the binding constraint is not the furnace, it is the special feedstock and gas. A scarce input caps how fast an 11% share can grow. One more comparison keeps me humble about scale: in the same trade-remedy file that records Birla Carbon's 30% to 34% capacity share, its ROCE is quoted at 36.7% for FY20, in a year when PCBL earned 16%. The definitions differ, so I would not push the gap too far, but it is the same industry in the same year.

Does the government protect the franchise? No, and this surprises many investors. India imposed anti-dumping duty on Chinese and Russian carbon black for years, and PCBL's FY2017 to FY2019 profits were earned behind it. On 22 December 2020 the trade remedies directorate recommended five more years, with a duty of US$494 a tonne on China. On 5 January 2021 the Finance Ministry declined. Since then there has been no protection. Imports of roughly 8,000 to 10,000 tonnes a month still pressured spot prices in October 2025, and the 2026 relief came from Russian refinery outages and firmer Chinese coal-tar prices, which can reverse. The only live anti-dumping case is Aquapharm's own petition on two phosphonates, and as of this report it is a recommendation rather than a notified duty.

There is one genuine tailwind I do not want you to miss. Western Europe imports about 500,000 tonnes of carbon black a year, and before the Russian ban about 80% of it came from Russia. CFO Raj Gupta said on 30 April 2026 that India now supplies close to 100,000 tonnes, and European Rubber Journal reports that India became the largest source of EU imports after the ban. That is a window opened by geopolitics, not by PCBL's skill. Mr Gupta was careful about the India–EU trade deal too: “there is no import duty on carbon black in Europe. So, there is no direct benefit.” The benefit is indirect, through tyre exports, where the EU's 4.5% duty on Indian tyres is likely to fall to zero. I treat the Europe window as a cost-advantage dividend that lasts as long as Russian supply stays impaired, and nobody can promise that.

That case reveals what Aquapharm's competitive position really is. The directorate found that the domestic industry, which includes Aquapharm, was making financial losses, cash losses and negative return on capital on those two products because Chinese landed prices were below its cost of sales. On 28 November 2023 Managing Director Kaushik Roy described Aquapharm as “one of the top two players” in phosphonates; by 2025 the wording had become “amongst Top 3”. I read the commodity end of phosphonates as a price-taker's business, and the value as sitting in customer-approved blends and green chelates, where the 2023 aim of “20x over the next 5 years” has produced about 1.2x in three years.

Battery materials deserves a sceptical, but not a dismissive, look. Group14's silicon-carbon plant at Moses Lake targets production in 2027 at 2,000 tonnes per module. Sila opened its plant in September 2025 after 14 years of research. Denka, Cabot, Orion and Imerys already sell conductive carbons into battery supply chains. PCBL's pilot plant started creating samples on 2 November 2026, after telling the market it would be “ready in the next few months” on 29 April 2025. On 15 May 2023 Mr Roy told investors that customer approvals would take “anywhere between say 6 months to 1 year or maybe a little more than 1 year but not like 3-4 years or something.” Three and a half years later, the first samples are under internal qualification. That is not failure, it is the normal speed of this industry, and it tells you the investment is an option rather than a moat.

So here is my verdict, stated the way I would say it to a colleague. PCBL has a narrow moat in Indian rubber-grade carbon black, built from port-side scale, co-generation and customer approvals. I give roughly two chances in three that this franchise earns its cost of capital through a full cycle, and well under one in three that it earns well above it. The peer who did earn well above, Himadri, raised its EBITDA margin from 6% to 22% in four years with ROCE of 32% and almost no net debt. PCBL's ROCE is 8%, about the same as its 7.8% cost of debt. The contrast is the Chairman's own sentence from 28 November 2023: “We have to shift platforms from Carbon Black.” You can respect the ambition and still note that the platform being left is the only one that has earned money so far.

If you hold this verdict, what would tell you early that you are wrong? I would watch five things, in this order. First, Indian capacity announcements: every additional 100,000 tonnes in a market running between 56% and 70% full makes a narrow moat narrower. Second, Russian refinery restarts, because the 2026 spot relief depends on them. Third, the crude path, because a sharp fall reverses inventory gains and tests the formula lag. Fourth, whether the HEDP and ATMP duty is notified, because that is the one live test of whether a trade remedy can lift Aquapharm's margin from 9.7%. Fifth, a named battery customer. None of these can be predicted, which is why I keep the verdict at narrow, not at none or moderate, and why I would rather re-read these five lines each quarter than defend a forecast.

Before you move on, remember the three parallels. Himadri shows what success on the same mechanism looks like. Venator shows what happens when margins collapse on borrowed money: adjusted EBITDA fell 71% and all $1,040 million of debt turned short-term. SRF shows that even excellent specialty chemical businesses reset after a peak, and SRF still earned a 21% EBITDA margin at its trough, against PCBL's 13.2%. In the next chapter I put management on trial: if the moat is narrow, the key performance indicators and the record of promises must carry the case.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A high margin in one quarter is a photograph; a moat is a film. PCBL's Q1 FY27 EBITDA per tonne of ₹22,900 was partly low-cost inventory, and Q2's ₹19,800 included a tariff refund worth ₹2,300 per tonne. Ask what survives when crude falls, when Russian supply returns and when the Indian capacity build-out arrives. The answer today is cost position, power and approvals: valuable, but narrow.

book_callouts.title: THE THREE-ARENA MOAT TEST
book_callouts.text: Score each arena separately, because a strength in one does not transfer to another.
bullets: Carbon black: narrow moat (scale, power, approvals) in an industry adding capacity twice as fast as demand.
Phosphonates and specialty chemicals: unproven; product-level losses at the DGTR period and EBITDA at 31% of the FY2026 forecast.
Battery materials: an option with no customer; leaders needed 14 years and hundreds of millions of dollars.
